text: If someone's DNA suddenly vanished, how long would that person last?
Nobody has ever lost all their DNA, so we can't say for sure what the precise sequence
of medical consequences would be.
But mushroom poisoning, chemotherapy, and radiation poisoning can give us a rough idea.
Amanita bisporigia is a species of mushroom found in eastern North America known by the
common name Destroying Angel.
If you're like me, you were told to never eat mushrooms you found in the woods.
Amanita is the reason why.
If you eat a Destroying Angel, for the rest of the day you'll feel fine.
Later that night, or the next morning, you'll suffer from vomiting, abdominal pain, and
severe diarrhea.
Then you'll start to feel better, at which point the damage is probably irreversible.
Amanita mushrooms contain amitoxin, which interferes with an enzyme used to read DNA,
interrupting the process by which cells follow DNA's instructions and causing irreversible
damage to whatever cells it collects in.
Since most of your body is made of cells, this is bad for you.
Death is generally caused by liver or kidney failure, since those are the first sensitive
organs in which the toxin accumulates.
Sometimes, intensive care and a liver transplant can be enough to save a patient, but often not.
The really frightening thing about Amanita poisoning is the walking ghost phase, the
period where you seem to be getting better, but your cells continue to accumulate irreversible
and lethal damage.
This pattern is typical of DNA damage, and we'd likely see something like it in someone
who lost their DNA.
The picture is even more vividly illustrated by two other examples of DNA damage, chemotherapy
and radiation.
Doxorubicin, one of the most common in potent chemotherapy drugs, interrupts cell division
by linking and tangling random sections of DNA together.
The reason Doxorubicin selectively kills cancer cells is that cancer cells are dividing all
the time, whereas most normal cells only divide occasionally.
Some human cells do divide nearly constantly, like those found in hair follicles, bone marrow
which produces blood, including white blood cells, and stomach lining.
Chemotherapy messes with the DNA of such constantly dividing cells and hampers cell
division, causing hair loss, vulnerability to infections, and, most immediately, nausea,
vomiting, and diarrhea.
Radiation poisoning also has a walking ghost phase, where the body is still working, but
no new proteins can be synthesized and the immune system is collapsing.
In cases of severe radiation poisoning, immune system collapses off in the primary cause of
death.
Without a supply of white blood cells, the body can't fight off infections, and ordinary
bacteria in the body run wild.
In short, losing your DNA would most likely result in abdominal pain, nausea, dizziness,
rapid immune system collapse, and death within days or hours from either rapid systemic
infection or system-wide organ failure.
On the other hand, there would be at least one silver lining.
If we ever end up in a dystopian future where an Orwellian, Gattaca-style police state collects
our genetic information and uses it to track and control us, you'd be invisible.
